evidence.quote: The family comprised 2 parents and 3 siblings. The parents and older brother had no history of kidney disease or extrarenal manifestations (Fig. 1a). An 11-year-old girl was diagnosed with proteinuria during a school urinary screening program, but she did not undergo further examination. At 18 years of age, she was referred to our nephrology department with an elevated serum creatinine (1.5 mg/dL). The patient did not present with any extrarenal manifestations. A kidney biopsy was not performed because of kidney atrophy. The patient was lost to follow-up, and when she was admitted to our hospital for loss of appetite at 19 years of age, she had progressed to ESKD, demonstrating the need for hemodialysis. She eventually underwent living KTx from her father when she was 20 years old. A zero-time renal biopsy revealed normal findings including podocyte mitochondria. Considering the rapid progression of kidney failure observed in this patient and proteinuria identified in her younger sister, next-generation and Sanger sequencing analysis was conducted to determine the origin of the kidney disease, which revealed a novel compound heterozygous mutation in the COQ8B gene (c.737G>A in exon 9 and c.1468C>T in exon 15) (Fig. 1b), leading to a diagnosis of COQ8B nephropathy (Fig. 2a). Five years after the KTx, recipient 1 developed de novo IgA nephropathy, which was successfully treated with prednisolone pulse therapy. The kidney function was serum creatinine 0.90 mg/dL and eGFR 63 mL/min/1.73 m^(2) at the final follow-up with normal urinalysis. The electronic microscopy of the transplanted kidney revealed normal findings of mitochondria in the podocytes, which denied post-transplant recurrence in the kidney graft. Kidney function of the donor was serum creatinine 1.24 mg/dL and eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m^(2) with normal urinalysis at the final follow-up.

summary.text: Recipient 1 had school-screening proteinuria at age 11 without further examination, nephrology referral at 18 for serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, and no extrarenal manifestations. Kidney atrophy prevented biopsy; she was lost to follow-up before admission with appetite loss and ESKD at 19, requiring hemodialysis. Table 1 reports eight years from onset to ESKD.

Living transplantation from her father occurred at age 20 with normal zero-time renal biopsy/podocyte mitochondria. Next-generation and Sanger sequencing confirmed compound heterozygous COQ8B c.737G>A and c.1468C>T; delayed diagnosis precluded CoQ10 treatment. Five years after transplant she developed de novo IgA nephropathy, successfully treated with prednisolone pulse therapy.

At final follow-up serum creatinine was 0.90 mg/dL, eGFR 63 mL/min/1.73 m² and urinalysis normal. Graft electron microscopy showed normal podocyte mitochondria without COQ8B recurrence; follow-up was five years.

evidence.quote: In general, the risk of living kidney donors developing ESKD is 3.5–5.3-fold higher than the projected risk in the absence of donation []. Transplant practitioners should pay utmost attention to the screening and selection of potential living donor candidates, especially in the clinical setting for kidney disease with a background of genetic disorders []. This is because living donors who are biologically related to the recipient have a higher risk of future kidney failure after kidney donation than unrelated donors []. However, transplant centers follow a case-by-case approach rather than a standard protocol for genetic assessment because of the lack of reliable evidence []. For example, it has been universally recognized that mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 genes are responsible for autosomal recessive Alport syndrome. However, individuals with pathogenic heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 variants have recently been diagnosed with thin basement membrane nephropathy or autosomal dominant Alport syndrome, and heterozygotes carrying certain mutation patterns are at a risk of future kidney dysfunction. In fact, the current guidelines for genetic testing and management of Alport syndrome state that COL4A3 and COL4A4 heterozygotes are not recommended as kidney donors in the development of late-onset kidney failure [–]. COQ8B nephropathy, similar to Alport syndrome, is an autosomal recessive hereditary kidney disease, though SRNS develops only in homozygotes and compound heterozygotes. To our knowledge, no cases of COQ8B nephropathy have been reported in individuals heterozygous for COQ8B variants. Our zero-time kidney biopsy specimens showing unaffected mitochondria in the podocytes and 5 or 2 years of an uneventful clinical course without dysuria or kidney dysfunction post-donation support the hypothesis that heterozygotes for COQ8B mutation can safely donate their kidneys. Nevertheless, the prognosis of COQ8B heterozygous donors has not been clarified so far, making it more important for our donors to maintain regular follow-ups.

Five years after the KTx, recipient 1 developed de novo IgA nephropathy, which was successfully treated with prednisolone pulse therapy. The kidney function was serum creatinine 0.90 mg/dL and eGFR 63 mL/min/1.73 m^(2) at the final follow-up with normal urinalysis. The electronic microscopy of the transplanted kidney revealed normal findings of mitochondria in the podocytes, which denied post-transplant recurrence in the kidney graft. Kidney function of the donor was serum creatinine 1.24 mg/dL and eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m^(2) with normal urinalysis at the final follow-up.

summary.text: The father, a documented heterozygous COQ8B carrier with no prior kidney disease or extrarenal manifestations, donated a kidney to his older daughter. Donation was uneventful. At final five-year follow-up serum creatinine was 1.24 mg/dL, eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m² and urinalysis normal; no dysuria or kidney dysfunction was reported. Regular donor follow-up was recommended because long-term heterozygote prognosis is uncertain.

events.description: Retrospective possible nonadherence explanation for CoQ10 failure, not confirmed

evidence.quote: A global cohort study demonstrated that supplementation with CoQ10 for primary CoQ10 deficiency due to biallelic pathogenic variants in either the COQ2, COQ6, or COQ8B genes led to better preservation of kidney function []. However, a nephroprotective effect was not observed in a subgroup of patients with COQ8B deficiency in this cohort, which had possibly been related to the typically late diagnosis and more advanced chronic kidney disease at treatment initiation. Song et al. [] retrospectively assessed 20 patients with COQ8B nephropathy and reported a significantly better kidney survival in early genetic detection group than that in delayed genetic detection group, enhancing the importance of early treatment. In fact, documented kidney responses vary from no response, partial remission, or complete disappearance of urinary protein [–], influenced by multiple factors such as delay in diagnosis, timing of therapy initiation, comorbid conditions, and variants in mutation []. Moreover, nonadherence rate is reported to be as high as 30–70% in pediatric populations [], making the treatment more complicated. In the present cases, late diagnosis of COQ8B nephropathy deprived the older sister of the opportunity for CoQ10 treatment, whereas the younger sister demonstrated little response to CoQ10 supplementation despite early diagnosis. Regarding the reasons for treatment failure, the younger sister was diagnosed at an early stage and received an adequate dose of CoQ10 supplementation. As for genetic mutations, this combination of compound heterozygous mutations (c.737G>A and c.1468C>T) is, to the best of our knowledge, the first genotype pattern reported to date, which may have been one of the factors for unresponsiveness. On the other hand, CoQ10 supplementation would have been effective if it had been initiated at an even earlier stage, that is, before the increase in proteinuria or serum creatinine. Nonadherence remains a differential diagnosis. An accumulation of cases is required to better understand the response to CoQ10 treatment in patients with COQ8B.

summary.text: Recipient 2 developed proteinuria at eight without extrarenal manifestations. After her older sister progressed to ESKD, kidney biopsy at eleven showed five of 30 sclerotic glomeruli and five with segmental sclerosis, FSGS, swollen granular tubular epithelial cells, podocyte foot-process effacement, abnormal increased mitochondria and microvillus transformation. Genetic testing found the same compound heterozygous COQ8B c.737G>A/c.1468C>T pattern.

CoQ10 started at 5 mg/kg/day and gradually increased to 30 mg/kg/day, but renal function, urinary protein and urinary β2-microglobulin deteriorated. Adding lisinopril 2.5 mg per day was not beneficial and ESKD developed. Nonadherence was only a possible author explanation, not an established behavior. Living transplantation from her mother occurred at sixteen, four years after treatment initiation.

Two years after transplantation serum creatinine was 1.02 mg/dL and eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73 m²; protocol kidney biopsy showed no disease recurrence. A normal recipient urinalysis is not reported for this later draw.

events.description: Regular donor follow-up recommended

evidence.quote: In general, the risk of living kidney donors developing ESKD is 3.5–5.3-fold higher than the projected risk in the absence of donation []. Transplant practitioners should pay utmost attention to the screening and selection of potential living donor candidates, especially in the clinical setting for kidney disease with a background of genetic disorders []. This is because living donors who are biologically related to the recipient have a higher risk of future kidney failure after kidney donation than unrelated donors []. However, transplant centers follow a case-by-case approach rather than a standard protocol for genetic assessment because of the lack of reliable evidence []. For example, it has been universally recognized that mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 genes are responsible for autosomal recessive Alport syndrome. However, individuals with pathogenic heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 variants have recently been diagnosed with thin basement membrane nephropathy or autosomal dominant Alport syndrome, and heterozygotes carrying certain mutation patterns are at a risk of future kidney dysfunction. In fact, the current guidelines for genetic testing and management of Alport syndrome state that COL4A3 and COL4A4 heterozygotes are not recommended as kidney donors in the development of late-onset kidney failure [–]. COQ8B nephropathy, similar to Alport syndrome, is an autosomal recessive hereditary kidney disease, though SRNS develops only in homozygotes and compound heterozygotes. To our knowledge, no cases of COQ8B nephropathy have been reported in individuals heterozygous for COQ8B variants. Our zero-time kidney biopsy specimens showing unaffected mitochondria in the podocytes and 5 or 2 years of an uneventful clinical course without dysuria or kidney dysfunction post-donation support the hypothesis that heterozygotes for COQ8B mutation can safely donate their kidneys. Nevertheless, the prognosis of COQ8B heterozygous donors has not been clarified so far, making it more important for our donors to maintain regular follow-ups.

summary.text: The mother, a heterozygous COQ8B carrier without prior kidney disease or extrarenal manifestations, donated a kidney to her younger daughter. At two-year follow-up serum creatinine was 0.93 mg/dL, eGFR 49 mL/min/1.73 m² and urinalysis normal; no dysuria or kidney dysfunction was reported. Donation was uneventful, and regular follow-up was recommended because heterozygote prognosis remains uncertain.
